cultivar: Mostly Da Ye oolong; also Jin Xuan and Qingxin Damou; small-leaf cultivars rather than Assam types
processing: Leafhopper-bitten summer leaf, withered long, rolled (often into small tight balls, sometimes strips), fully oxidised and dried; no roast and no pesticides, because the insects must be allowed to feed.
harvest_season: Summer (June–September), when the tea green leafhopper is active, carries the most honey; small spring lots are lighter.
appearance_dry: Small, tightly rolled dark balls or short twisted strips with golden tips, smelling strongly of honey.
appearance_wet: Small, even copper-brown leaves with ragged, bitten edges.
taste_profile: Honey, ripe longan and a touch of muscat on a soft, sweet, low-astringency body; a black tea that needs nothing added.

brewing.notes: Around 90 °C with short gongfu steeps or three minutes Western-style; boiling water and long steeps hide the honey. One of the best cold-brew teas Taiwan makes.

vintage_note: Sold by summer harvest year, with June-to-September leaf carrying the most honey, from Ruisui producers and increasingly from Taitung, Mingjian and the Alishan foothills; the Ruisui farmers' association runs an evaluation that grades local lots. The word 'honey' is used freely, so bitten leaf edges and a honey-scented empty cup are the check. Drink it within two years.
description:
Mi Xiang black, 'honey-fragrance black tea', is the signature tea of the east coast: a small-leaf black from the Wuhe terrace in Ruisui, Hualien, made from summer leaf that the tea green leafhopper has fed on. The insect bites trigger the plant's honey-scented defence compounds, the same mechanism behind Oriental Beauty, and full oxidation turns that into a black tea that tastes like a spoonful of honey without any being added.

The style was worked out in Ruisui in the 2000s, when farmers on the terrace, which sits at only 200 to 300 metres near the Tropic of Cancer marker, were looking for something to do with bug-bitten summer leaf that was worthless as oolong. The leaf is mostly Da Ye oolong, with some Jin Xuan and Qing Xin Da Mou: withered long, rolled, often into small tight balls, fully oxidised and dried, with no roast and no pesticides, because the hoppers have to be allowed to feed.

The cup is bright orange-amber and tastes of honey, ripe longan and a touch of muscat on a soft, sweet body with almost no astringency; it is a black tea that needs nothing added and is gentle enough for the evening. Brew it at around 90 degrees with short gongfu steeps or three minutes Western-style; boiling water and long steeps do no great harm but hide the honey. It is one of the best cold-brew teas Taiwan makes.

It is sold by summer harvest year, with the June-to-September leaf carrying the most honey, from Ruisui producers and, increasingly, from Taitung, Mingjian and the Alishan foothills, where the same idea is applied to Si Ji Chun and Jin Xuan. The Ruisui farmers' association runs an evaluation that grades local lots. The word 'honey' is used freely, so look for the ragged, bitten edges on the wet leaf and an empty cup that smells of honey; a lot with neither is just a pleasant small-leaf black. Drink it within two years.

If you like it, Ruby 18 from the same island is the bold, minty opposite, and Mi Xiang oolong is the same leaf stopped halfway.
sources_note: The 2000s Ruisui origin and the farmers' association evaluation are from memory; the cultivar mix on the Wuhe terrace (Da Ye oolong dominant) is my best understanding.
